blocks.text: General
In a liquid medium (blood), gases are present in 2 forms: - the dissolved form - the combined form
The dissolved fraction is the only form of gas that participates in the partial pressure.
General

The volume of a gas dissolved in a liquid is determined by: - ??its partial pressure - its solubility coefficient - the temperature of the liquid. It is calculated from the dissolution law or Henry's law: Vgaz = ? x Pgaz/ Patm
where ? represents the solubility coefficient
Gas diffuses from an area of ??high pressure to an area of ??low pressure. This fundamental law governs the transport of gases in the body.
Transport of O2 in the blood

1- General view of the transport of O2 in the blood The lungs and the cardiovascular system = system allowing the tissuees to be supplied with O2. The quantity of O2 supplied to the tissuees depends on: - the quantity of O2 entering the lungs - the quality of gas exchanges at the alveolar level - blood supply to the tissuees depending on the degree of constriction of the vessels and cardiac output - the capacity for transport of O2 in the blood determined by the quantity of dissolved O2, the hemoglobin content of the blood and the affinity of hemoglobin for O2.

Transport of O2 in the blood
1- General view of the transport of O2 in the blood

In arterial blood, PaO2:- slightly lower than that of alveolar air. - is 100 mm Hg - decreases with age In venous blood, PvO2: - depends on the organs and the intensity of metabolism. - is on average 40 mm Hg.
Transport of O2 in the blood
2- Dissolved O2
The quantity of dissolved O2 is directly proportional to PO2 (Henry's law). the higher the PO2, the more O2 dissolved in the plasma. - Dissolved fraction of O2 = 1.5% of O2 in the blood.
At the arterial level, for a normal PaO2 of 100 mm Hg, there are 3 ml of dissolved O2 per liter of blood; i.e. 15 ml/min of dissolved O2 for a cardiac output of 5 l/min.
Transport of O2 in the blood

2- Dissolved O2 At rest, O2 consumption - = 250 ml / min - increases up to 25 times during physical exercise. another mode of transport of O2 in the blood = hemoglobin. O2 combined with hemoglobin:- = 98.5% - does not contribute to the PO2 of the blood. PO2 only reflects the fraction of O2 dissolved and not the quantity of O2 in the blood.

5- Oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve - Between 60 and 100 mm Hg PO2, the curve is in plateau and the Hb saturation is 97.5%, almost almost complete saturation. If PO2 decreases below the normal value, Hb saturation decreases little and so does the O2 content of the blood. Plateau of the curve = a safety margin for the transport of O2 by the blood. This segment corresponds to the area of ??PO2 in the pulmonary capillaries. - Between 0 and 60 mm Hg PO2: curve with a segment
abrupt where O2 is discharged from Hb. This segment corresponds to the PO2 zone in the systemic capillaries.
Transport of O2 in the blood
5- Oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve

PO2 at 50% O2 saturation, called P50, is a useful measure of the position of the hemoglobin dissociation curve. Its normal value in humans is 27 mm Hg. Three points should be noted on the curve: - normal arterial blood with a PO2 100, SO2 97% - normal venous blood with a PO2 40, SO2 75% - P50 27, SO2 50%

6- Factors modifying the HbO2 dissociation curve
- PCO2 and the concentration of H+ ions
- the temperature
- the concentration of 2,3 diphosphoglycerate (2,3-DPG)
Transport of O2 in the blood
6- Factors modifying the HbO2 dissociation curve
Increase in these factors = shift in the curve of
dissociation to the right signifying a decrease in affinity
of Hb for O2.
Drop in one of these factors = shift of the curve towards
the left with increased affinity of Hb for O2.
Transport of O2 in the blood
6- Factors modifying the HBO2 dissociation curve
a- Effect of PCO2 and H+ ion concentration
CO2 diffuses from tissuees to blood increasing PCO2
as well as the release of H+ ions with a decrease in blood pH;
which shifts the Hb dissociation curve to the right.
This results in a drop in the affinity of Hb for O2 with
increased supply of the latter to the tissuees. This phenomenon is
known as the Bohr effect. The decrease in PCO2 and the
concentration of H+ ions has an opposite effect moving the
curve to the left with increase in the affinity of
hemoglobin for O2.

blocks.text: Transport of O2 in the blood
6- Factors modifying the dissociation curve of HBO2b- Effect of 2,3-diphosphoglycerate
One mole of 2,3-DPG binds to one mole of Hb depending on the reaction
following:
HbO2 + 2,3-DPG Hb-2,3-DPG + O2
Any increase in the concentration of 2,3-DPG shifts the
reaction and the dissociation curve of Hb to the right
leading to a release of O2 into the blood.
The drop in concentration of 2,3-DPG shifts the curve towards
the left with a decrease in the P50 hence an increase in
the affinity of Hb for O2.
Transport of O2 in the blood
6- Factors modifying the HBO2 dissociation curve
c- Effect of temperature
The rise in temperature following the production of
heat through tissuee metabolism promotes dissociation
of O2 of Hb and leads to a shift of the curve towards
the right.
Transport of CO2 in the blood
1- General view of CO2 transport
Cellular metabolism produces 200 ml/min of CO2 which
diffuses towards the blood and is carried by the latter under 3
shapes:
- in dissolved form
- in combined form with hemoglobin
- in the form of bicarbonates
Total blood CO2 = dissolved CO2 + Hb-bound CO2 + HCO3-
Transport of CO2 in the blood
2- Under dissolved CO2
The quantity of dissolved CO2 obeys Henry's law and depends
of the PCO2 partial pressure.
Dissolved CO2 represents 10% of the total blood content in
CO2. It is 24 times more soluble than O2.
Transport of CO2 in the blood
3- CO2 combined with hemoglobin
CO2 binds to Hb globin to form
carbaminohemoglobin according to the following reaction:
Hb-NH2 + CO2 Hb-NH-COOH
CO2 in this form represents 30% of CO2
contained in the blood.
Transport of CO2 in the blood
4- CO2 in the form of bicarbonates
HCO3- is the predominant transport of CO2
representing 60% of the CO2 contained in the blood.
In the erythrocyte, CO2 is converted to HCO3-
following the formula:
CO2 + H2O H2CO3 H+ + HCO3-
carbonic anhydrase

1- Relationship between pH, PCO2 and HCO3- of plasma
In the body, [H+] = 40nmol/l corresponding to a neutral pH of
- Acidic solution if pH < 7.4 with [H+] > 40 nmol/l.
- Alkaline solution if pH > 7.4 with [H+] < 40 nmol/l.
- A pH < 6.9 or > 7.8 is incompatible with life.
The pH is given by the Henderson-Hasselbach equation:
pH = 6.1 + log [HCO3- ] / [H2CO3]
pH = 6.1 + log [HCO3- ]/CO2
pH = 6.1 + log [HCO3- ]/PCO2x0.03
The relationship between pH, PCO2 and HCO3- is represented by the
pH-bicarbonate diagram or Davenport diagram.
